title: How Generative AI Is Reshaping Professional Liability Risk for Law Firms
author: AnneMarie McPherson Spears

dom.t: Malpractice insurance: Reported AI claims remain hard to isolate

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source accepts the supervised-tool model, emphasizing verification, human professional judgment, confidentiality safeguards and formal governance. It materially extends the cluster by connecting failures of oversight to professional-liability coverage and arguing that existing policies generally remain adequate when human review and protocols are maintained.
qs: “I don’t think we need policies to evolve to address AI coverage on an express basis, because the policies will perform in the utilization of AI as a tool where human oversight, review and protocols are in place.”  Of course, AI’s continued development may mean the discussion looks entirely different in a year.

“For now, it remains largely a check-the-box inquiry as underwriters continue to monitor how AI adoption evolves.”  Burke recommends that law firms implement AI governance frameworks that define permissible use and verification standards while ensuring audit trails of AI-generated content are maintained.

st.t: AI insurance: Coverage cannot replace professional governance
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core proposition that professional liability coverage may accommodate appropriately supervised AI use but cannot substitute for professional governance. It makes coverage contingent on human oversight, review and protocols, recommends verification standards and audit trails, and treats denial after extreme verification failure as a possible insurer argument rather than settled law.
qs: “I don’t think we need policies to evolve to address AI coverage on an express basis, because the policies will perform in the utilization of AI as a tool where human oversight, review and protocols are in place.”  Of course, AI’s continued development may mean the discussion looks entirely different in a year.

“For now, it remains largely a check-the-box inquiry as underwriters continue to monitor how AI adoption evolves.”  Burke recommends that law firms implement AI governance frameworks that define permissible use and verification standards while ensuring audit trails of AI-generated content are maintained.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s principal proposition by presenting legal AI as capable of reducing costs and turnaround times while stressing that its value depends on correct use. Its sanctions example and warnings about unreliable output, eroded professional judgment, standards of care and ethics reinforce the cluster’s emphasis on verification and user competence, though it offers no concrete workflow controls or evidence about broader organisational and labour effects.

st.t: Malpractice insurance: Reported AI claims remain hard to isolate
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s cautious account: it treats sanctions as illustrations rather than coverage outcomes, says appropriately supervised AI use generally remains covered, raises only a hypothetical coverage challenge for extreme verification failures, and frames tighter underwriting for firms without documented controls as a prediction rather than an established pricing effect. It provides no claims-incidence data, consistent with the cluster’s conclusion that AI losses remain difficult to isolate.
qs: “Underwriters are indicating that when firms use AI appropriately, coverage will extend to claims that involve an AI-related component.”  In an extreme scenario, “if a firm files a brief containing citations to six fictitious cases and the court determines that adequate verification was not performed, the question becomes whether such conduct constitutes a legal service rendered to the client.

We anticipate that over the next to 12 to 18 months, firms without documented protocols will fall out of preferred-risk tiers and will not secure the most competitive terms.”  [AnneMarie McPherson Spears*](mailto:annemarie.mcpherson@iiaba.net)* is IA news editor.*

st.an: The source supports the cluster’s qualified account of operational gains and the need for verification, professional judgment and compliance controls. Its evidence is limited to law firms and a reported sanctions incident, so it does not substantively address bargaining shifts toward legal departments, ALSPs or AI-native providers, or contested pricing change.

kp.k: Fabricated AI quotations have triggered substantial court sanctions
kp.d: The article reports, citing NBC News, that a California court ordered an attorney to pay a $10,000 fine in September 2025 for a state court appeal containing 21 fake quotations generated by ChatGPT. It describes the fine as the largest issued to date over AI fabrications and presents the incident as one of multiple legal hallucination cases, not a measurement of model error rates.
qs: In September 2025, a California court ordered an attorney to pay a $10,000 fine for filing a state court appeal that contained 21 fake quotations generated by ChatGPT, according to NBC News.

kp.k: AI efficiency benefits accompany professional judgment and compliance risks
kp.d: Sean Burke, senior broker at Jencap, says law firms increasingly rely on AI for reduced costs, faster turnaround and access to analytics. He conditions its benefits on correct use and identifies dependence on AI accuracy, erosion of professional judgment, and compliance with standards of care and ethical requirements as accompanying risks. These are practitioner assertions rather than quantified findings.
qs: You have reduced costs, improved turnaround times and access to analytics. When it’s utilized correctly, it’s incredibly powerful.

dependence on AI for accuracy and reliability, whether your professional judgment is being eroded, and whether you’re meeting the standard of care and ethical codes that the American Bar Association (ABA) and equivalent regulators require of law firms

kp.k: Existing liability policies generally lack express AI exclusions
kp.d: Burke says the vast majority of law firm professional liability policies do not expressly exclude AI. He reports underwriter indications that claims involving AI will be covered when firms use it appropriately. He considers explicit policy changes unnecessary where AI remains a tool subject to human oversight, review and protocols; this is his assessment, not a coverage ruling.
qs: From an insurance perspective, the vast majority of law firm professional liability policies do not have express AI exclusions, Burke says.
Underwriters are indicating that when firms use AI appropriately, coverage will extend to claims that involve an AI-related component.

I don’t think we need policies to evolve to address AI coverage on an express basis, because the policies will perform in the utilization of AI as a tool where human oversight, review and protocols are in place.

kp.k: Inadequate verification could provoke disputes over covered legal services
kp.d: Burke offers a hypothetical brief citing six fictitious cases, with a court finding inadequate verification, to question whether the conduct would qualify as a legal service under liability coverage. He speculates that an insurer could regard it as outside recognized legal practice rather than insured negligence in performing legal services. The article does not report an actual coverage denial or establish this interpretation as law.
qs: if a firm files a brief containing citations to six fictitious cases and the court determines that adequate verification was not performed, the question becomes whether such conduct constitutes a legal service rendered to the client. Does it satisfy the standard of care, or does it place the attorney outside the bounds of recognized legal practice?

I think a carrier would say, ‘This is not the intent of providing insurance for negligence in the performing of a legal service, because you’re outside the construct of a legal service at that point,’

kp.k: Underwriting inquiries remain limited as regulatory exposures may evolve
kp.d: Burke recommends that independent insurance agents ask law firm clients how they use AI during renewals. He characterizes current underwriting scrutiny as largely a check-the-box inquiry while adoption is monitored. Separately, he predicts that generative AI's development may prompt regulatory oversight or standards introducing exposures not currently present, without identifying specific future rules.
qs: How are you utilizing AI?
For now, it remains largely a check-the-box inquiry as underwriters continue to monitor how AI adoption evolves.
The pace of generative AI will drive certain regulatory oversight or standards that may bring certain exposures that don’t exist today

kp.k: Governance should document permissible uses, verification and audit trails
kp.d: Burke recommends AI governance frameworks specifying permitted uses and verification standards, with retained audit trails of AI-generated content. He also favors closed-system AI, attributing credibility, plagiarism and client confidentiality concerns to open-system AI's use of supplied information. These are risk-management recommendations rather than demonstrated comparative findings about system types.
qs: Burke recommends that law firms implement AI governance frameworks that define permissible use and verification standards while ensuring audit trails of AI-generated content are maintained.
He also stresses the importance of using closed-system AI, as open-system AI’s use of inputted information introduces credibility and plagiarism concerns, as well as client confidentiality issues.

kp.k: Client disclosure and sign-off are recommended claims protections
kp.d: Burke recommends that insurance agents encourage law firms to disclose AI use to clients. He describes client sign-off as protection against future claims, without asserting that it eliminates liability or replaces verification obligations.
qs: Agents should also encourage law firms to disclose AI usage to clients.
Client sign-off is a great protection against a future claim

kp.k: Undocumented protocols may jeopardize preferred insurance terms
kp.d: In the March 9, 2026 article, Burke predicts that firms with appropriate AI controls should remain well-positioned, while firms without documented protocols will lose preferred-risk status and access to the most competitive insurance terms over the next 12 to 18 months. This is a forward-looking underwriting expectation, not a reported change already observed.
qs: Firms that adopt appropriate AI controls should remain well-positioned. We anticipate that over the next to 12 to 18 months, firms without documented protocols will fall out of preferred-risk tiers and will not secure the most competitive terms.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: AI offers operational benefits but creates verification, professional-judgment and confidentiality risks; appropriate controls may determine both coverage expectations and future insurance terms.
pts.d: Sean Burke, senior broker at Jencap, says law firms increasingly rely on AI because it reduces costs, improves turnaround times and provides analytics when used correctly. He identifies risks involving accuracy, reliability, erosion of professional judgment, and compliance with standards of care and ethical requirements. Author AnneMarie McPherson Spears reports a sanctions incident involving AI-generated quotations and predicts further hallucination incidents. Burke says most law firm professional liability policies lack express AI exclusions and reports underwriter indications that appropriately used AI will be covered. He speculates that an extreme failure to verify fictitious citations could prompt a carrier to argue the conduct falls outside a covered legal service; this is a hypothetical coverage position, not a reported determination. He does not think express AI-specific policy changes are necessary where human oversight, review and protocols exist. He predicts that AI development could generate new regulatory standards and exposures, and that firms without documented protocols will lose preferred-risk status and competitive terms. He recommends governance, verification standards, audit trails, closed-system AI and client disclosure, presenting these as risk protections. His claim that open-system AI introduces credibility, plagiarism and confidentiality concerns is not accompanied by a technical account of particular systems.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source relies on one reported sanctions incident and an insurance broker’s professional observations, reported underwriter indications and forecasts.
pts.d: Spears cites NBC News for a September 2025 California court sanction: a $10,000 fine for an appeal containing 21 fabricated quotations generated by ChatGPT. This is an example of a hallucination-related sanctions incident, not a measured model error rate or evidence of an insurance coverage outcome. Burke supplies the operational-benefit and insurance-market claims as an interviewed broker. His account of policy exclusions and underwriting practice is not supported in the article by a policy sample, survey or quantitative market data. The six-fictitious-cases scenario is explicitly hypothetical. The article provides no measured productivity gains, adjudicated AI coverage dispute, or empirical estimate of how much governance or client sign-off reduces claims. The prediction about preferred-risk tiers is attributed to Burke, rather than presented as an observed market change.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current benefits and coverage expectations are conditional on appropriate use and human oversight; underwriting differentiation is forecast over the following 12–18 months.
pts.d: The article is dated March 9, 2026, and its sanctions example concerns September 2025. It describes increasing adoption, mostly absent express AI exclusions and largely check-the-box underwriting inquiries as current conditions. Burke conditions benefits on correct use and coverage expectations on appropriate use, oversight, review and protocols. His suggested coverage challenge depends on an extreme scenario involving fictitious citations and a court finding that adequate verification was not performed; he does not claim that all AI mistakes negate coverage. Spears says the discussion could look different in a year, while Burke links potential new exposures to the pace of AI development and consequent regulatory oversight or standards. Burke explicitly forecasts loss of preferred-risk tiers and competitive terms for firms without documented protocols over the next 12–18 months, approximately through March–September 2027. He qualifies his reassurance for controlled firms as a suspicion and an expectation, not a guarantee.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Law firms and attorneys face operational opportunities, professional risks and possible insurance-market consequences; clients, insurers and independent agents have distinct roles.
pts.d: Law firms using AI are the principal affected providers: they may gain lower costs, faster turnaround and analytics, but face professional liability and governance requirements. Individual attorneys can face court sanctions for unverified fabricated material. Burke distinguishes firms with appropriate documented controls from firms without them, predicting less favorable insurance positioning for the latter without distinguishing firm size or practice area. Clients face confidentiality concerns and are the intended recipients of AI-use disclosure and requests for sign-off. Insurers and underwriters monitor adoption, assess controls and may confront coverage questions; independent insurance agents are advised to ask about AI at renewal and encourage governance and disclosure. The article does not make claims about lawyer headcount, staffing structures, ALSP competition or access to justice.
